# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

### 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) replaces the existing study-room reservation tool across three university libraries. Students and staff must be able to search rooms and equipment, create or change reservations, cancel reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff must manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms display the current and next reservation.

CLRS integrates with three external systems:

- The university identity provider through SAML.
- Facilities calendars through iCal feeds.
- A legacy, read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

The most important quality concerns are availability, search performance, authentication and auditing, configuration-based onboarding of new campuses, testability of reservation rules, and simple operational deployment. The system must provide 99.5% monthly availability during opening hours, support availability-search p95 latency below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users, and allow a two-person team to deploy and roll back within ten minutes.

This design selects **hexagonal architecture as the primary style**, implemented initially as a modular monolith. It separates the framework-independent reservation domain from HTTP, persistence, SAML, iCal

# 48433 Software Architecture — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and library staff across three campuses. Students must be able to search for rooms and equipment, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Staff must manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms must display current and upcoming reservations.

The system integrates with three external systems:

- the university identity provider through SAML;
- facilities-calendar iCal feeds;
- the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

The most important quality constraints are 99.5% availability during opening hours, search latency below 400 ms at the 95th percentile with 2,000 concurrent users, SAML authentication and staff auditing, configuration-only onboarding of new campuses, database-independent testing of reservation rules, and deployment or rollback by a two-person team within ten minutes.

This design selects a **hexagonal architecture with a modular monolith** as the primary style. Hexagonal boundaries isolate the reservation domain from HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, notification
